newsitem.title: albania: Albanians want Berisha out before yielding arms.
newsitem.headline: Albanians want Berisha out before yielding arms.

text.p: Rebels in southern Albania, who have seized thousands of army weapons during a 10-day uprising, said on Tuesday that President Sali Berisha must resign before they surrender their arms.
"Weapons won't be turned in without guarantees. Our basic demand is for Berisha to resign," said Fuad Karali, chief of rebel police in this southern port.
The revolt has brought the southwest corner of Albania under rebel control, from the Adriatic ports of Vlore and Sarande to the inland towns of Delvine, Gjirokaster, Tepelene, Permet and Berat.
Vlore rebels have agreed to Berisha's deal with opposition parties to hold new elections by June, but rebels elsewhere were defiant and rejected any compromise while the president stayed in power.

Some 150,000 assault rifles have been looted from barracks during a week of rage. Tanks, anti-aircraft guns, heavy cannon and even fighter jets were seized and guard the approaches to the rebel towns.
"Every family in southern Albania has at least one assault rifle," said Limpi Mango, a rebel leader in Permet, which fell on Sunday.
"One town after the next is falling to the people. It would be crazy to surrender our weapons. It would be like accepting defeat while you're winning," he said.
Berisha has agreed to form an all-party government, hold elections and grant amnesty to all those involved in the revolt. On Sunday he gave the rebels a week to put down their weapons.

"We'll see what kind of government emerges because Berisha will certainly try to control it. This new government must have widespread approval if rebels are to give up their guns," said Besnik Sehu, the socialist opposition party representative in Gjirokaster.
"There may be some differences among rebel leaders but we are united in calling for Berisha to go. Everybody lost money in the pyramid schemes and nobody trusts him any more," he added.
Thousands of Albanians lost their savings when five popular pyramid investment schemes collapsed in January, plunging the Balkan country into crisis.
The pyramid failure sparked widespread anti-government riots and protests which turned into an armed revolt.
Only the Vlore rebels have accepted Berisha's proposal and signed an Italian-brokered deal to return their weapons.

"I am surprised with Vlore's decision," said Horin Hasani, another rebel in Gjirokaster. "I don't know of any other town ready to do the same. In any case nobody has the power at this point to enforce the weapons' return."
He added: "If we give up our weapons, Berisha will send in his secret police to slaughter us. This is the way things work in Albania."
Rebel councils have restored some order to Sarande, Berat, Tepelene and Gjirokaster, laying down rules to stop wild shooting, punish looting and set a curfew.

Despite those rules, hundreds of people in Sarande looted an eight-storey state hotel all day on Tuesday, packing cars and trucks with everything from furniture, toilet seats and blankets to windows, doors and broken electrical appliances.
The looters then set fire to the hotel.
Aristide Hoxha, a small hotel owner nearby, said: "I have two Kalashnikovs and will shoot anybody close to my property."

Hoxha said that so many weapons had been stolen from state arsenals in recent days that it would be impossible to persuade people to give them back. "Nobody will return the weapons even if Berisha resigns," he said.
Reporters returning from Permet on Monday were forced at gunpoint to give petrol to the owner of a car stranded by the road.
